claim: Before the outbreak that reached the Americas in 2015, Zika virus (ZIKV) circulated in Asia and the Pacific.
source: Before the outbreak that reached the Americas in 2015, Zika virus (ZIKV) circulated in Asia and the Pacific: these past epidemics can be highly informative on the key parameters driving virus transmission, such as the basic reproduction number (R0).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by references to historical outbreaks in the introduction.

claim: R0 for the Pacific ZIKV epidemics is estimated between 1.5 and 4.1.
source: R0 for the Pacific ZIKV epidemics is estimated between 1.5 and 4.1, the smallest islands displaying higher and more variable values.
evidence: This estimate is derived from the modeling analysis presented in the results section, with specific values shown in Tables 1-2 and Figures 2-3.

claim: The smallest islands display higher and more variable R0 values.
source: R0 for the Pacific ZIKV epidemics is estimated between 1.5 and 4.1, the smallest islands displaying higher and more variable values.
evidence: This observation is supported by the data in Tables 1-2 showing Yap (smallest population) has the highest R0 estimates.

claim: This relatively low range of R0 suggests that intervention strategies developed for other flaviviruses should enable as, if not more effective control of ZIKV.
source: This relatively low range of R0 suggests that intervention strategies developed for other flaviviruses should enable as, if not more effective control of ZIKV.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the comparison of estimated R0 values with other flaviviruses.

claim: In May 2015, the first local cases of Zika were recorded in Brazil.
source: In May 2015, the first local cases of Zika were recorded in Brazil and by December of the same year the number of cases had surpassed 1.5 million.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the timeline of the Zika outbreak in Brazil.

claim: By December 2015, the number of Zika cases in Brazil had surpassed 1.5 million.
source: In May 2015, the first local cases of Zika were recorded in Brazil and by December of the same year the number of cases had surpassed 1.5 million.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the scale of the outbreak.

claim: On February 2016, the World Health Organization declared Zika as a public health emergency of international concern.
source: On February 2016, the World Health Organization declared Zika as a public health emergency of international concern (Who, 2016)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to WHO 2016.

claim: In March 2016, local transmission of Zika was recognized in 34 countries.
source: in March 2016, local transmission of Zika was recognized in 34 countries.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the geographic spread of Zika.

claim: In 2007 the outbreak on Yap (Micronesia) was the first Zika outbreak outside Africa and Asia.
source: In 2007 the outbreak on Yap (Micronesia) was the first Zika outbreak outside Africa and Asia (Duffy et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Duffy et al., 2009.

claim: Zika outbreaks have been reported in French Polynesia and in New Caledonia between 2013 and 2014.
source: Since, Zika outbreaks have been also reported in French Polynesia and in New Caledonia (Cao-Lormeau et al., 2014; Dupont-Rouzeyrol et al., 2015) between 2013 and 2014
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cao-Lormeau et al., 2014 and Dupont-Rouzeyrol et al., 2015.

claim: Zika virus (ZIKV) is a flavivirus, mostly transmitted via the bites of infected Aedes mosquitoes.
source: Zika virus (ZIKV) is a flavivirus, mostly transmitted via the bites of infected Aedes mosquitoes, although non-vector-borne transmission has been documented (sexual and maternofoetal transmission, laboratory contamination, transmission through transfusion) (Musso and Gubler, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Musso and Gubler, 2016.

claim: Non-vector-borne transmission of ZIKV has been documented, including sexual and maternofoetal transmission, laboratory contamination, and transmission through transfusion.
source: Zika virus (ZIKV) is a flavivirus, mostly transmitted via the bites of infected Aedes mosquitoes, although non-vector-borne transmission has been documented (sexual and maternofoetal transmission, laboratory contamination, transmission through transfusion) (Musso and Gubler, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Musso and Gubler, 2016.

claim: The most common clinical manifestations of ZIKV include rash, fever, arthralgia, and conjunctivitis.
source: The most common clinical manifestations include rash, fever, arthralgia, and conjunctivitis (Musso and Gubler, 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Musso and Gubler, 2016.

claim: A large proportion of ZIKV infections are asymptomatic or trigger mild symptoms that can remain unnoticed.
source: but a large proportion of infections are asymptomatic or trigger mild symptoms that can remain unnoticed.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about ZIKV infection characteristics.

claim: ZIKV may be involved in Guillain-Barre syndrome.
source: Nevertheless, the virus may be involved in many severe neurological complications, including Guillain-Barre syndrome (Cao-Lormeau et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cao-Lormeau et al., 2016.

claim: ZIKV may be involved in microcephaly in newborns.
source: and microcephaly in newborns (Schuler-Faccini et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schuler-Faccini et al., 2015.

claim: The basic reproduction number (R0) is defined as the average number of secondary cases caused by one typical infected individual in an entirely susceptible population.
source: Defined as the average number of secondary cases caused by one typical infected individual in an entirely susceptible population, the basic reproduction number (R0) is a central parameter in epidemiology used to quantify the magnitude of ongoing outbreaks and it provides insight when designing control interventions (Diekmann et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a standard definition supported by citation to Diekmann et al., 2010.

claim: R0 is a central parameter in epidemiology used to quantify the magnitude of ongoing outbreaks and provides insight when designing control interventions.
source: Defined as the average number of secondary cases caused by one typical infected individual in an entirely susceptible population, the basic reproduction number (R0) is a central parameter in epidemiology used to quantify the magnitude of ongoing outbreaks and it provides insight when designing control interventions (Diekmann et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Diekmann et al., 2010.

claim: R0 is complex to estimate.
source: It is nevertheless complex to estimate (Diekmann et al., 2010; van den Driessche and Watmough, 2002)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Diekmann et al., 2010 and van den Driessche and Watmough, 2002.

claim: Two compartmental models with vector-borne transmission are compared in this study.
source: Two compartmental models with vector-borne transmission are compared (cf. Figure 1).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Both models use a Susceptible-Exposed-Infected-Resistant (SEIR) framework to describe the virus transmission in the human population.
source: Both models use a Susceptible-Exposed-Infected-Resistant (SEIR) framework to describe the virus transmission in the human population, but differ in their representation of the mosquito population.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the description of the models.

claim: The Pandey model formulates explicitly the mosquito population, with a Susceptible-Exposed-Infected (SEI) dynamic to account for the extrinsic incubation period.
source: Figure 1a is a schematic representation derived from Pandey et al. (2013) and formulates explicitly the mosquito population, with a Susceptible-Exposed-Infected (SEI) dynamic to account for the extrinsic incubation period (time taken for viral dissemination within the mosquito).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and shown in Figure 1a, with citation to Pandey et al., 2013.

claim: In the Laneri model, the vector is modeled implicitly using compartments κ and λ representing the force of infection for vector to human transmission.
source: By contrast, in the second model (Figure 1b) based on Laneri et al. (2010) the vector is modeled implicitly: the two compartments κ and λ do not represent the mosquito population but the force of infection for vector to human transmission.
evidence: This is explicitly stated and shown in Figure 1b, with citation to Laneri et al., 2010.

claim: During the 2007 outbreak in Yap, 108 suspected or confirmed Zika cases (16 per 1000 inhabitants) were reported.
source: During the 2007 outbreak that struck Yap, 108 suspected or confirmed Zika cases (16 per 1000 inhabitants) were reported by reviewing medical records and conducting prospective surveillance between April 1st and July 29th 2007 (Duffy et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Duffy et al., 2009.

claim: In French Polynesia, sentinel surveillance recorded more than 8700 suspected cases (32 per 1000 inhabitants) across the whole territory between October 2013 and April 2014.
source: In French Polynesia, sentinel surveillance recorded more than 8700 suspected cases (32 per 1000 inhabitants) across the whole territory between October 2013 and April 2014 (CHSP, 2014; Mallet et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to CHSP, 2014 and Mallet et al., 2015.

claim: In New Caledonia, approximately 2500 cases (9 per 1000 inhabitants) were reported through surveillance between January and August 2014.
source: In New Caledonia, the first Zika case was imported from French Polynesia on 2013 November 12th. Approximately 2500 cases (9 per 1000 inhabitants) were reported through surveillance between January (first autochtonous case) and August 2014 (DASS, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to DASS, 2014.

claim: In Yap, a household survey conducted after the epidemic yielded an infection rate of 73%.
source: In Yap, a household survey was conducted after the epidemic, yielding an infection rate in the island of 73% (Duffy et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Duffy et al., 2009.

claim: In French Polynesia, a seroprevalence study conducted before the Zika outbreak concluded that most of the population was naive for Zika virus.
source: In French Polynesia, three seroprevalence studies were conducted. The first one took place before the Zika outbreak, and concluded that most of the population was naive for Zika virus (Aubry et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Aubry et al., 2015a.

claim: A seroprevalence survey conducted in French Polynesia between February and March 2014 reported a seroprevalence rate around 49%.
source: The second seroprevalence survey was conducted between February and March 2014, at the end of the outbreak, and reported a seroprevalence rate around 49% (Aubry et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Aubry et al., 2015b.

claim: All models are simulated in a discrete stochastic framework to take into account the high variability in transmission rates due to small population size.
source: Therefore all these models are simulated in a discrete stochastic framework (Poisson with stochastic rates [Bretó et al., 2009]), to take this phenomenon into account.
evidence: This is explicitly stated with citation to Bretó et al., 2009.

claim: Estimations are performed with PMCMC algorithm (particle Markov Chain Monte Carlo).
source: Stochasticity requires specific inference techniques: thus estimations are performed with PMCMC algorithm (particle Markov Chain Monte Carlo [Andrieu et al., 2010]).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with citation to Andrieu et al., 2010.

claim: The estimates of R0 lie between 1.6 (1.5–1.7) and 3.2 (2.4–4.1) and vary notably with respect to settings and models.
source: Our estimates of R0 lie between 1.6 (1.5–1.7) and 3.2 (2.4–4.1) and vary notably with respect to settings and models (Figures 2–3 and Tables 1–2).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figures 2-3 and Tables 1-2.

claim: Yap displays consistently higher values of R0 in both models.
source: Strikingly, Yap displays consistently higher values of R0 in both models
evidence: This is supported by the data in Tables 1-2.

claim: There is an inverse relationship between island size and both the value and variability of R0.
source: and in general, there is an inverse relationship between island size and both the value and variability of R0.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern observed in the data across different islands.

claim: The two highly connected islands in French Polynesia, Tahiti and Moorea, display similar R0 values despite their differing sizes.
source: However, the two highly connected islands in French Polynesia, Tahiti and Moorea, display similar values despite their differing sizes.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Tables 1-2.

claim: R0 estimates are always higher and coarser with the Pandey model than with the Laneri model.
source: Regarding model variability, R0 estimates are always higher and coarser with the Pandey model than with the Laneri model (cf. Tables 1–2).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of the data in Tables 1-2.

claim: The Pandey model has two additional estimated parameters compared to the Laneri model, including the mosquito lifespan, which can explain the higher variability of the output.
source: The Pandey model has two additional estimated parameters (in particular, the mosquito lifespan), which can explain the higher variability of the output.
evidence: This is an inference based on the model structure and results.

claim: The mosquito lifespan parameter is very sensitive in the Pandey model.
source: It is worth noting that these parameters are very sensitive (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by the sensitivity analysis presented in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The initial number of infected individuals (HI(0)) is higher in the Laneri model than in the Pandey model.
source: The difference in R0 may also be linked to the difference in the estimated initial number of infected individuals (HI(0)), which is higher in the Laneri model than in the Pandey model.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Tables 1-2.

claim: The ratio of asymptomatic to symptomatic ZIKV cases is estimated to be 1:1.3.
source: Because of the high proportion of asymptomatic cases (the ratio of asymptomatic:symptomatic is estimated to be 1:1.3, V.-M Cao-Lormeau personal communication)
evidence: This is based on personal communication from V.-M Cao-Lormeau.

claim: For the durations of infectious and intrinsic incubation (in human) and extrinsic incubation (in mosquito) periods, the posterior density resembles the informative prior.
source: For the durations of infectious and intrinsic incubation (in human) and extrinsic incubation (in mosquito) periods, the posterior density ressembles the informative prior (cf. Figures 6–13), indicating the models' incapacity to identify properly these parameters without more informative data.
evidence: This is supported by the posterior distributions shown in Figures 6-13.

claim: The fraction ρ of the population involved in the epidemic is well estimated when the seroprevalence is known (in Yap and French Polynesia).
source: The fraction ρ of the population involved in the epidemic is well estimated when the seroprevalence is known (in Yap and French Polynesia).
evidence: This is supported by the narrow confidence intervals for ρ in these settings as shown in Tables 1-2.

claim: In Yap and French Polynesia, the proportion of the population involved is slightly greater than the seroprevalence rate, indicating a very high infection rate among involved individuals.
source: In these cases, the proportion of the population involved is slightly greater than the seroprevalence rate, indicating a very high infection rate among involved individuals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of estimated ρ values with observed seroprevalence rates.

claim: In New Caledonia, the fraction of population involved displays very large confidence intervals, indicating that the model did not manage to identify properly this parameter with the available data.
source: In New Caledonia, as no information on seroprevalence was available, the fraction of population involved displays very large confidence intervals (cf. Tables 1 and 2), indicating that the model did not manage to identify properly this parameter with the available data.
evidence: This is supported by the wide confidence intervals shown in Tables 1-2.

claim: In New Caledonia, the observation rate r and the fraction of population involved ρ are highly correlated and seem unidentifiable without precise information on seroprevalence.
source: In this case, this parameter is highly correlated to the observation rate r (cf Figures 17 and 21): r and ρ seem unidentifiable without precise information on seroprevalence.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation plots in Figures 17 and 21.

claim: R0 can be used to inform public health authorities on the level of risk posed by an infectious disease, vaccination strategy, and the potential effects of control interventions.
source: R0 can be used to inform public health authorities on the level of risk posed by an infectious disease, vaccination strategy, and the potential effects of control interventions (Anderson and May, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Anderson and May, 1982.

claim: Using a similar version of the Pandey model in French Polynesia, Kucharski et al. estimated R0 between 1.6 and 2.3 for Tahiti and between 1.8 and 2.9 in Moorea.
source: Using a similar version of the Pandey model in French Polynesia, Kucharski et al. (Kucharski et al., 2016) estimated R0 between 1.6 and 2.3 (after scaling to square root for comparison) for Tahiti and between 1.8 and 2.9 in Moorea.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kucharski et al., 2016.

claim: Kucharski et al. predicted a seroprevalence rate at the end of the epidemic of 95–97%, far from the 49% measured.
source: Moreover, they predicted a seroprevalence rate at the end of the epidemic of 95–97%, far from the 49% measured.
evidence: This is a comparison with results from Kucharski et al., 2016.

claim: A study by Funk et al. used a very detailed deterministic mosquito model and estimated an R0 for Zika in Yap island between 2.9 and 8.
source: In Yap island, a study (Funk et al., 2016) used a very detailed deterministic mosquito model, and estimated an R0 for Zika between 2.9 and 8.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Funk et al., 2016.

claim: A study by Nishiura et al. relied on a method for R0 calculation based on the early exponential growth rate of the epidemic in French Polynesia and Yap.
source: Finally, a third study (Nishiura et al., 2016a) relied on another method for R0 calculation (based on the early exponential growth rate of the epidemic) in French Polynesia as a whole and in Yap.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nishiura et al., 2016a.

claim: The estimates of R0 for ZIKV are similar to but generally on the lower side of estimates made for dengue and Yellow Fever viruses.
source: On a final note, the estimates of R0 for ZIKV are similar to but generally on the lower side of estimates made for two other flaviviruses of medical importance, dengue and Yellow Fever viruses (Favier et al., 2006; Imai et al., 2015; Massad et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Favier et al., 2006; Imai et al., 2015; Massad et al., 2003.

claim: Two recent studies indicated that sexual transmission alone is not sufficient to sustain a ZIKV epidemic.
source: Even though further work and data are needed to support this hypothesis (Brauer et al., 2016), two recent studies indicated that sexual transmission alone is not sufficient to sustain an epidemic (Gao et al., 2016; Towers et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gao et al., 2016 and Towers et al., 2016.

claim: The Zika outbreak in Yap occurred with a different ZIKV lineage than in French Polynesia and New Caledonia.
source: Moreover, whilst both New Caledonia and French Polynesia populations were infected by the same ZIKV lineage and transmitted by the same principle vector species, Aedes aegypti, the epidemic in Yap occurred much earlier with a different ZIKV lineage (Wang et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2016.

claim: The Zika outbreak in Yap was vectored by Aedes hensilli.
source: and vectored by a different mosquito species Aedes hensilli (Ledermann et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ledermann et al., 2014.

claim: Both New Caledonia and French Polynesia populations were infected by the same ZIKV lineage and transmitted by the same principle vector species, Aedes aegypti.
source: Moreover, whilst both New Caledonia and French Polynesia populations were infected by the same ZIKV lineage and transmitted by the same principle vector species, Aedes aegypti
evidence: This is stated as a fact comparing the outbreaks.

claim: In French Polynesia, the vector Aedes polynesiensis is also present and dominates in Moorea with higher densities than in Tahiti.
source: In French Polynesia, the vector Aedes polynesiensis is also present and dominates in Moorea with higher densities than in Tahiti.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about vector distribution.

claim: The first Zika case in New Caledonia was imported from French Polynesia on November 12th, 2013.
source: In New Caledonia, the first Zika case was imported from French Polynesia on 2013 November 12th.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the timeline of the outbreak.

claim: Only a fraction ρ of the total population is involved in the epidemic, due to spatial heterogeneity, immuno-resistance, or cross-immunity.
source: In addition, we consider that only a fraction ρ of the total population is involved in the epidemic, due to spatial heterogeneity, immuno-resistance, or cross-immunity.
evidence: This is a modeling assumption to account for observed patterns.

claim: For both models, N=ρ⋅H with H the total size of the population reported by census.
source: For both models we define N=ρ⋅H with H the total size of the population reported by census.
evidence: This is an explicit definition used in the models.

claim: The estimated seroprevalence at the end of the epidemic in Yap using the Pandey model is 73% (CI95: 68–77), compared to the observed 73%.
source: The estimated seroprevalences at the end of the epidemic (with 95% credibility intervals) are: (a) 73% (CI95: 68–77, observed 73%)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 caption.

claim: The estimated seroprevalence at the end of the epidemic in Moorea using the Pandey model is 49% (CI95: 45–53), compared to the observed 49%.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 caption.

claim: The estimated seroprevalence at the end of the epidemic in Tahiti using the Pandey model is 49% (CI95: 45–53), compared to the observed 49%.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 caption.

claim: The estimated seroprevalence at the end of the epidemic in New Caledonia using the Pandey model is 39% (CI95: 8–92).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 caption.

claim: The estimated seroprevalence at the end of the epidemic in Yap using the Laneri model is 72% (CI95: 68–77), compared to the observed 73%.
source: The estimated seroprevalences at the end of the epidemic (with 95% credibility intervals) are: (a) 72% (CI95: 68–77, observed 73%)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3 caption.

claim: The estimated seroprevalence at the end of the epidemic in New Caledonia using the Laneri model is 65% (CI95: 24–91).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3 caption.

claim: For the Pandey model in Yap, the basic reproduction number R0 is estimated as 3.2 (2.4–4.1).
source: Basic reproduction number R0 3.2 (2.4–4.1)
evidence: This is shown in Table 1.

claim: For the Laneri model in Yap, the basic reproduction number R0 is estimated as 2.2 (1.9–2.6).
source: Basic reproduction number R0 2.2 (1.9–2.6)
evidence: This is shown in Table 2.

claim: The study highlights the importance of seroprevalence data for precise quantitative analysis of pathogen propagation.
source: Our study also highlights the importance of seroprevalence data for precise quantitative analysis of pathogen propagation, to design prevention and control strategies.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis, particularly regarding parameter identifiability.

claim: The Zika outbreak was concomitant with dengue outbreaks in French Polynesia.
source: The Zika outbreak was concomitant with dengue outbreaks in French Polynesia (CHSP, 2014; Mallet et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to CHSP, 2014 and Mallet et al., 2015.

claim: The Zika outbreak was concomitant with dengue outbreaks in New Caledonia.
source: and New Caledonia (DASS, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to DASS, 2014.

claim: Examples of coinfection between Zika and dengue have been reported.
source: Examples of coinfection have been reported (Dupont-Rouzeyrol et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dupont-Rouzeyrol et al., 2015.

claim: For all criteria in the sensitivity analysis, the key parameters in both models are transmission parameters (R0 and βV).
source: For all criteria, the key parameters in both models are transmission parameters (R0 and βV).
evidence: This is based on the sensitivity analysis results presented in Tables 6-7.

claim: High values for R0 are positively correlated with a large seroprevalence and a high and early peak.
source: High values for R0 are positively correlated with a large seroprevalence and a high and early peak.
evidence: This is based on the sensitivity analysis results.

claim: The fraction involved in the epidemic (ρ) influences the magnitude of the outbreak but has no significant effect on the timing of the peak.
source: As expected, the fraction involved in the epidemic (ρ) influences the magnitude of the outbreak, by calibrating the proportion of people than can be infected, but it has no significant effect on the timing of the peak.
evidence: This is based on the sensitivity analysis results.

claim: The estimation tools are provided by the open source software SSM (State Space Models).
source: The estimation tools are provided by the open source software SSM (Dureau et al., 2013) (State Space Models, RRID:SCR_014647), available at https://github.com/JDureau/ssm and https://github.com/sballesteros/ssm-predict.
evidence: This is explicitly stated with citation to Dureau et al., 2013.
